content:
It's the weekend and given the recent conversations, now seems like a good time to mention https://mattrobball.github.io/BridgelandStability/ which is a project formalizing Tom Bridgeland's 2007 Annals paper introducing stability conditions on triangulated category and proving they form a complex manifold. The notion of a stability conditions is based on @Michael R Douglas's Π\PiΠ-stability for D-branes and work on them is now one of the most active areas in modern mathematics.

While it is interesting that today's models are good enough to successfully formalize top notch modern Annals papers in domains outside the penumbra of Mathlib, I don't think it is that surprising to anyone who has been experimenting with them. So getting to working code is only part of the story.

The main goal is better understand how to work productively with these models to produce honest human insight and reusable, quality code. A side-effect of this is to encourage behavior and set norms that are beneficial to the formalization and broader mathematical communities.

To these ends, let me highlight the following aspects of the project:

  1. Issues are open to anyone to comment and claude and codex are plugged in to take handoffs of tasks. (Note: I need to call them though). Mathematicians, non-mathematicians, lean-experts, non-lean-experts are all welcome to come, file issues, and help drive this experiment in AI-assisted formalization. Not all the paper is formalized and the code can definitely be improved so there is a lot one can do, or prod the agents to do.
  2. Comparator is wired up to the main result from Bridgeland's paper (Corollary 1.3) and we use tooling that makes it easy to expose all data carrying declarations that feed into the statement of the challenge result. This is all displayed on a subpage https://mattrobball.github.io/BridgelandStability/comparator/ of the project webpage. There you will find Verso-annotated Lean code for all 50ish of the statements you need to believe to trust that end result. This is easier to audit than the 34k lines of code. There is also a lean playground TFB generator that is inbound, see the static one for now.
  3. We include a new schema for documenting formalization projects formalization.yaml which tries to present a more standardized, language-agnostic view of such projects with fields that cover review, tooling, compute, and roles. You should find the answers to standard questions about such projects there. And if you don't, it might need an update.
  4. There is tooling to track and maintain semantic alignment between the formal and informal statements. Similar to the comparator setup, this is intended to lessen human cognitive overhead when reviewing changes so one doesn't have to hold the whole project mentally to avoid breaking the existing alignment. The landing page for the project tracks declarations that have exact matches.

There is an ongoing discussion at https://github.com/mattrobball/BridgelandStability/issues/41 to improve accessibility to the content for the non-lean-fluent.

Like the formalization itself, the other aspects of the project are an experiment to figure out what works well and what doesn't. Arguably these are going to be most important moving forward.

If this interests you, please consider engaging. Apologies for not having a Zenodo link ;)
Very cool! This direction went far beyond the physics inspiration and there is a lot to do here both for math and for physics. Looking forward to seeing what formalization and Lean can contribute!
